fields.meta_title: COBRA Election Form: Deadlines and an App | Emergent
fields.meta_description: What a COBRA election form asks, the 60-day and 45-day deadlines behind it, and an app that tracks every election for HR.
fields.h1: Build a COBRA Election Form That Tracks Every Deadline
fields.hero_description: A COBRA election form lets a former employee and their family keep the employer's health plan. Describe your process, and Emergent builds the form and the deadline tracking behind it.
fields.features_heading: Every Deadline the Election Form Carries
fields.features_subheading: The model notice explains the rules in prose. This version counts the days per person, from the right start date.
fields.feature_1:
One election row per beneficiary

Lists every person the plan covered, from the former employee to a spouse and each child, and records a separate choice for each. A spouse can keep medical while a child declines it.
fields.feature_2:
Windows that start on the right day

Picks the start of each 60-day window from the two dates on file and shows a day count beside every open election. HR can sort the dashboard by the days each person has left.
fields.feature_3:
Premiums shown with the admin fee

Shows each monthly premium with the fee included, beside the first payment date 45 days after the election. Later months show the 30-day grace period and when each payment is due.
fields.feature_4:
Waivers that can be taken back

Records each waiver with its date and lets the person revoke it while the election period is open. HR sees both dates on one row instead of piecing them together from email.
fields.feature_5:
Signed elections with a timestamp

Captures each beneficiary's e-signature and saves the coverage choices with the time they arrived, in a database you own. No election depends on a PDF sitting in an email thread.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take to your HRIS

Exports the full code to your GitHub on paid plans. An engineer can wire elections into your benefits platform's API, or you can describe the change and Emergent writes it for you.

fields.usecase_heading: Every Step of a COBRA Election
fields.tab_content_1:
Spouse, children, and employee each decide

A layoff ends coverage for everyone on the employee's plan. Federal rules give each qualified beneficiary their own right to elect, and the form lists everyone the plan covered. Jordan Ellis keeps medical and dental, her spouse keeps medical only, and her son declines. HR receives one signed row per person.
fields.tab_content_2:
Ten days left and still no election

The clock does not always start when the letter goes out. Each 60-day window runs from the later of two dates: the day coverage ended or the day the notice was sent. When a former employee reaches day 50 with no reply, Emergent emails a reminder and flags the row for HR.
fields.tab_content_3:
The premium up front and 45 days to pay

Under COBRA the former employee usually pays the employer's share along with their own. Right after Kim Tran elects, the form shows the plan's $618.00 monthly cost, an administrative fee of $12.36 and a premium of $630.36. Plans can add a fee of up to 2%. The first payment is due 45 days after the election.
fields.tab_content_4:
After a divorce, 14 days to send the notice

Divorce changes who the plan covers. Sam Patel reports it through the form and attaches the decree. Benefits lead Maya Chen gets a Slack direct message: the notice for Alex Rivera is due within 14 days. As an ex-spouse, Alex can keep coverage for up to 36 months.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a COBRA Election Form
fields.howto_description: The form itself is short. The real work is in the deadlines behind it, and the seven steps follow the order a plan administrator meets them.
fields.howto_step_1_des: The Department of Labor publishes a model election notice with an election form at the end, and plans fill in the blanks. Keep its order of sections, then add your plan's name, the administrator's contact details, and every coverage option the employee had.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Include each person the plan covered the day before the qualifying event: the employee, a spouse, and any dependent children. Give each one a row and a choice, since every qualified beneficiary may elect or decline independently of the others.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Count 60 days from coverage loss or from the notice, whichever is later. Print the actual deadline date on the form instead of restating the rule. Nobody filling it in at home should have to work out the arithmetic themselves.
fields.howto_step_4_des: State the monthly premium for each coverage choice, which may run up to 102% of what the plan pays. Give the first payment deadline, 45 days after the election, and the 30-day grace period that applies to every month after that.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Offer a waiver and a way back
fields.howto_step_5_des: Include a box to waive coverage. A person who waives can still revoke the waiver before the election period ends, and coverage may then start on that date, depending on the plan. Record the date of each waiver and each revocation.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Ask each adult beneficiary to sign and date the election. Confirm a current mailing address as well, because premium invoices and the notice of when coverage ends go there long after the employee has left the building.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Decide who watches open elections and unpaid first premiums, and who answers questions. Print that person's name and phone number on the form, then review open elections every week until each one is elected, waived or expired.

claims_to_source: COBRA applies to group health plans of private employers with 20 or more employees
Qualified beneficiaries have 60 days to elect, starting from the later of the date coverage ends or the date the election notice is provided
A plan must give at least 45 days after the election to make the first premium payment, and a 30-day grace period for later payments
Coverage lasts up to 18 months after job loss or reduced hours, and up to 36 months after death, divorce or legal separation, or Medicare enrollment
The premium cannot exceed 102 percent of the plan's cost, so a former employee usually pays the full premium plus two percent
Each qualified beneficiary may elect COBRA independently
Job loss qualifies except for gross misconduct

The employer has 30 days to notify the plan and the plan has 14 days to send the election notice; for divorce or a child losing dependent status the employee or beneficiary must notify the plan within 60 days
Coverage may start on the election date or be retroactive to the date coverage ended, depending on plan terms, and a waiver can be revoked during the election period
The DOL publishes a model election notice that plan administrators fill in, ending with an election form
Losing job-based coverage opens a 60-day Special Enrollment Period in the Marketplace, where savings depend on household income
